# Overview



Molly.jl is a pure Julia package designed for molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and the study of physical systems more broadly. Built from first principles in Julia, it provides a modular, high-performance framework for exploring molecular behavior from noble gases to biological macromolecules. The package emphasizes **extensibility**, **performance**, and **reproducibility**, making it particularly suitable for both research applications and educational purposes.

![Molly logo](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/blob/master/docs/src/images/logo_molly.png)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L15), [src/Molly.jl](/src/Molly.jl#L1-L74)

## Key Features

Molly.jl implements a comprehensive suite of molecular simulation capabilities, distinguishing itself through several unique features in the Julia ecosystem:

| Category | Features |
|----------|----------|
| **Non-bonded Interactions** | Lennard-Jones, Coulomb potential, reaction field, gravitational potential, soft sphere, Mie, Buckingham potentials, soft core variants for alchemical simulation |
| **Bonded Interactions** | Harmonic and Morse bonds, bond angles, torsion angles, harmonic position restraints, FENE bonds |
| **Electrostatics** | Ewald and Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) summation methods |
| **Integration Methods** | Verlet, Velocity Verlet, Störmer-Verlet, flexible Langevin, Nosé-Hoover integrators |
| **Temperature Control** | Andersen, Berendsen, and velocity rescaling thermostats |
| **Pressure Control** | C-rescale, Monte Carlo, and Berendsen barostats |
| **Constraints** | SHAKE and RATTLE constraint algorithms |
| **Boundary Conditions** | Periodic, triclinic, and infinite boundary conditions |
| **Optimization** | Steepest descent energy minimization |
| **Advanced Methods** | Replica exchange molecular dynamics (REMD), Monte Carlo simulation |
| **Performance** | Automatic multithreading, GPU acceleration (CUDA, other KernelAbstractions backends), neighbor list algorithms, cell list implementation via CellListMap.jl |
| **Analysis & I/O** | Flexible loggers, trajectory output (DCD, XTC via Chemfiles.jl), OpenMM force field file reading, RDF and other analysis functions |
| **Integration** | Unitful.jl compatibility, AtomsBase.jl and AtomsCalculators.jl interfaces, Python ASE calculator interface |
| **Differentiable** | **Unique feature**: full automatic differentiation support via Enzyme.jl for force field optimization and gradient-based parameter learning |
| **Visualization** | Animation support with Makie.jl |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L17-L52), [Project.toml](/Project.toml#L1-L89)

## Architecture Overview

Molly.jl follows a **modular design principle** where all major components of a simulation can be customized. The architecture centers around the `System` object, which encapsulates all simulation state, and the `simulate!` function, which orchestrates time evolution.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Core System"
        SYS[System]
        A[Atoms]
        C[Coordinates]
        V[Velocities]
        B[Boundary]
    end
    
    subgraph "Interactions"
        PI[Pairwise Interactions]
        SI[Specific Interactions]
        GI[General Interactions]
    end
    
    subgraph "Simulation Control"
        SIM[Simulators]
        TH[Thermostats]
        BA[Barostats]
        CON[Constraints]
    end
    
    subgraph "Infrastructure"
        NF[Neighbor Finders]
        LOG[Loggers]
        BUF[Buffers]
    end
    
    SYS --> A
    SYS --> C
    SYS --> V
    SYS --> B
    SYS --> PI
    SYS --> SI
    SYS --> GI
    SYS --> NF
    SYS --> LOG
    
    SIM --> SYS
    TH --> SIM
    BA --> SIM
    CON --> SIM
    
    PI --> BUF
    NF --> BUF
```

Sources: [src/types.jl](/src/types.jl#L1-L150), [src/Molly.jl](/src/Molly.jl#L1-L74)

## Modular Component System

The package's power derives from its extensible interface design. Each component category follows specific patterns that allow users to define custom implementations with the same performance characteristics as built-in versions.

**Interaction Types** follow a hierarchical type system rooted in `AbstractInteraction`. Pairwise interactions (between all or most atom pairs) subtype `PairwiseInteraction`, which is an alias for `NBodyInteraction{2}`. Specific interactions between predetermined atom groups use `InteractionListNAtoms` types where N specifies the atom count (1 for position restraints, 2 for bonds, 3 for angles, 4 for torsions).

Sources: [src/types.jl](/src/types.jl#L1-L80)

**The System Object** serves as the central data structure containing atoms, coordinates, velocities, boundary conditions, interactions, constraints, neighbor finders, loggers, and unit specifications. It implements the `AtomsBase.AbstractSystem` interface for interoperability with the broader Julia molecular simulation ecosystem. The System can run on CPU or GPU arrays, with automatic type inference determining the appropriate code paths.

Sources: [src/types.jl](/src/types.jl#L900-L1100), [docs/src/documentation.md](/docs/src/documentation.md#L65-L95)

**Simulators** define the time evolution algorithm. Built-in options include deterministic integrators (VelocityVerlet, Verlet, StörmerVerlet), stochastic integrators (Langevin variants), minimization (SteepestDescentMinimizer), and advanced sampling (TemperatureREMD, HamiltonianREMD, MetropolisMonteCarlo). Custom simulators implement the `simulate!` function interface.

Sources: [src/simulators.jl](/src/simulators.jl#L1-L100)

## Performance Architecture

Molly.jl achieves competitive performance through several architectural decisions:

**CPU Optimization** leverages Julia's native multithreading capabilities with automatic parallelization of force calculations and neighbor finding. StaticArrays store coordinates and velocities for stack-allocated small vectors, avoiding heap allocation overhead during inner loops.

**GPU Acceleration** uses KernelAbstractions.jl for cross-platform GPU support, with optimized CUDA kernels in the `MollyCUDAExt` extension. The implementation employs warp-level operations and Morton code spatial sorting for efficient neighbor finding on GPUs. Cell list algorithms reduce the O(N²) pairwise complexity to approximately O(N) for sparse systems.

**Neighbor Finding** provides multiple strategies including brute force (NoNeighborFinder), distance-based cell lists, and more sophisticated algorithms for large systems. The neighbor finder automatically updates periodically to balance accuracy and performance.

Sources: [ext/MollyCUDAExt.jl](/ext/MollyCUDAExt.jl#L1-L200), [README.md](/README.md#L17-L52)

## Extension System

Molly.jl uses Julia's package extension system to provide optional functionality:

| Extension | Purpose | Key Dependencies |
|-----------|---------|------------------|
| MollyCUDAExt | GPU acceleration on NVIDIA devices | CUDA.jl, KernelAbstractions.jl |
| MollyEnzymeExt | Automatic differentiation | Enzyme.jl |
| MollyGLMakieExt | Interactive visualization | GLMakie.jl, Colors.jl |
| MollyKernelDensityExt | Density estimation | KernelDensity.jl |
| MollyPythonCallExt | Python interoperability | PythonCall.jl |

This design allows users to install only the extensions they need, keeping the core package lightweight while enabling powerful capabilities when required.

Sources: [Project.toml](/Project.toml#L42-L57)

## Differentiable Simulation

A **unique and defining feature** of Molly.jl is full support for differentiable molecular dynamics. Through the Enzyme.jl integration, gradients can be computed through entire simulations with respect to force field parameters, atomic coordinates, or other system properties. This capability enables:

- Gradient-based force field optimization
- Inverse design of molecular systems
- Neural network-enhanced potentials trained end-to-end
- Sensitivity analysis of simulation outcomes

The differentiability is achieved without sacrificing the performance optimizations described above, making it practical for research applications requiring many gradient evaluations.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L17-L52), [Project.toml](/Project.toml#L46-L47)

## Quick Start Example

The following example demonstrates Molly.jl's core workflow for simulating a Lennard-Jones fluid:

```julia
using Molly

# Define atoms with LJ parameters
n_atoms = 100
atom_mass = 10.0u"g/mol"
atoms = [Atom(mass=atom_mass, σ=0.3u"nm", ϵ=0.2u"kJ * mol^-1") for i in 1:n_atoms]

# Set up simulation box and initial conditions
boundary = CubicBoundary(2.0u"nm")
coords = place_atoms(n_atoms, boundary; min_dist=0.3u"nm")
temp = 298.0u"K"
velocities = [random_velocity(atom_mass, temp) for i in 1:n_atoms]

# Configure interactions and simulator
pairwise_inters = (LennardJones(),)
simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.002u"ps",
    coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 1.0u"ps"),
)

# Create system and run simulation
sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=pairwise_inters,
    loggers=(temp=TemperatureLogger(100),),
)

simulate!(sys, simulator, 10_000)
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L54-L85), [docs/src/documentation.md](/docs/src/documentation.md#L20-L70)

## Installation

Molly.jl requires Julia 1.10 or later. Install from the Julia REPL in package mode:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.add("Molly")
```

For GPU acceleration, install the appropriate backend package (e.g., `Pkg.add("CUDA")` for NVIDIA GPUs). The optional extensions are loaded automatically when the corresponding packages are available.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L86-L92)

## Example Applications

The package demonstrates versatility across application domains:

**Biomolecular Simulation** can simulate proteins with full atomic detail, reading OpenMM force fields and running PME electrostatics for accurate long-range interactions. GPU acceleration enables microsecond-scale simulations of biologically relevant systems.

![Protein simulation](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/raw/master/docs/src/images/sim_6mrr.gif)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L100-L130)

**Materials Science** applications include crystal systems via SimpleCrystals.jl integration, polymer chains with bonded interactions, and implicit solvent methods for solvation free energies.

**Exotic Systems** like gravitational many-body problems demonstrate Molly's flexibility beyond traditional molecular dynamics. The solar system simulation example shows how custom potentials can model planetary orbits.

Sources: [docs/src/examples.md](/docs/src/examples.md#L50-L100)

> [!TIP]
> The modular design allows you to mix and match components—use GPU-accelerated pairwise forces with CPU-based specific interactions, or combine deterministic integrators with stochastic thermostats. This flexibility enables experiments that would be difficult in more monolithic MD packages.

## Development and Community

Molly.jl maintains an active development roadmap and welcomes contributions. The package follows semantic versioning but notes that API stability is not yet guaranteed as it approaches maturity. Key areas for community contribution include new interaction types, simulators, performance optimizations, and example applications.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L131-L160), [docs/src/development.md](/docs/src/development.md#L1-L18)

# Quick Start



Welcome to Molly.jl, a pure Julia package for molecular dynamics simulation. This guide will get you running your first MD simulation in minutes. Molly enables simulation of physical systems ranging from noble gases to biological macromolecules, with built-in support for GPU acceleration, automatic differentiation, and a wide range of force fields.

![Molly logo](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/blob/master/docs/src/images/logo_molly.png)

## System Architecture

Understanding Molly's core architecture helps you structure your simulations effectively. The system follows a modular design where each component handles a specific aspect of the simulation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph System["System Object"]
        A[Atoms<br/>mass, charge, σ, ϵ]
        C[Coordinates<br/>positions]
        V[Velocities<br/>momentum]
        B[Boundary<br/>periodic box]
        I[Interactions<br/>forces]
        L[Loggers<br/>observables]
        N[Neighbor Finder<br/>optimization]
    end
    
    subgraph Simulation["Simulation Control"]
        S[Simulator<br/>integrator]
        T[Couplers<br/>thermostat/barostat]
    end
    
    I --> F[Force Calculation]
    S --> U[Time Integration]
    T --> W[Temperature/Pressure Control]
    
    F --> U
    W --> U
    U --> C
    U --> V
    
    C --> L
    V --> L
    F --> L
    
    style System fill:#e1f5ff
    style Simulation fill:#fff4e1
```

The **System** object encapsulates your complete molecular system state, while the **Simulation** components control how that state evolves through time. This separation makes it easy to experiment with different integrators and coupling schemes while keeping the underlying physics consistent.

## Installation

Get started with Molly in just a few commands. Molly requires **Julia 1.10 or later** for the latest features and best performance.

Install from the Julia REPL:
```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.add("Molly")
```

For GPU acceleration, install the appropriate backend (e.g., CUDA for NVIDIA GPUs):
```julia
Pkg.add("CUDA")
```

Verify your installation with a simple import:
```julia
using Molly
```

Sources: [Project.toml](Project.toml#L1-L30), [README.md](README.md#L40-L45)

## Your First Simulation: Lennard-Jones Fluid

Let's simulate a simple Lennard-Jones fluid—100 argon-like atoms interacting through van der Waals forces. This example demonstrates the complete workflow from system setup to simulation execution.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Define System Parameters] --> B[Create Atoms]
    B --> C[Generate Coordinates]
    C --> D[Initialize Velocities]
    D --> E[Setup Interactions]
    E --> F[Configure Simulator]
    F --> G[Run Simulation]
    G --> H[Analyze Results]
    
    style A fill:#f0f0f0
    style H fill:#d4edda
```

### Complete Simulation Code

```julia
using Molly

# System parameters
n_atoms = 100
boundary = CubicBoundary(2.0u"nm")        # Periodic cubic box
temp = 298.0u"K"                          # Temperature
atom_mass = 10.0u"g/mol"                  # Atom mass

# Create atoms with Lennard-Jones parameters
atoms = [Atom(
    mass=atom_mass, 
    σ=0.3u"nm",      # Distance parameter
    ϵ=0.2u"kJ * mol^-1"  # Energy well depth
) for i in 1:n_atoms]

# Place atoms randomly, avoiding overlap
coords = place_atoms(n_atoms, boundary; min_dist=0.3u"nm")

# Initialize velocities from Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
velocities = [random_velocity(atom_mass, temp) for i in 1:n_atoms]

# Define pairwise interactions
pairwise_inters = (LennardJones(use_neighbors=true),)

# Create neighbor finder for efficiency
neighbor_finder = DistanceNeighborFinder(
    eligible=trues(n_atoms, n_atoms),
    n_steps=10,
    dist_cutoff=2.0u"nm",
)

# Configure integrator with temperature control
simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.002u"ps",                             # 2 femtosecond timestep
    coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 1.0u"ps"),  # Thermostat
)

# Set up loggers to track properties
loggers = (
    temp=TemperatureLogger(100),              # Log every 100 steps
    coords=CoordinatesLogger(100),            # Track positions
    energy=TotalEnergyLogger(100),            # Track energy
)

# Assemble complete system
sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=pairwise_inters,
    neighbor_finder=neighbor_finder,
    loggers=loggers,
)

# Run simulation for 10,000 steps (20 ps)
simulate!(sys, simulator, 10_000)

# Access logged results
println("Final temperature: ", last(values(sys.loggers.temp)))
println("Final energy: ", last(values(sys.loggers.energy)))
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L47-L72), [test/simulation.jl](test/simulation.jl#L17-L56)

### Key Components Explained

| Component | Purpose | Example Values |
|-----------|---------|----------------|
| **Atoms** | Define particle properties | `mass`, `σ`, `ϵ`, `charge` |
| **Coordinates** | 3D positions with units | `SVector(0.5, 0.3, 0.7)u"nm"` |
| **Boundary** | Simulation box type | `CubicBoundary`, `RectangularBoundary` |
| **Interactions** | Force calculation rules | `LennardJones`, `Coulomb`, bond/angle potentials |
| **Simulator** | Integration algorithm | `VelocityVerlet`, `Langevin` |
| **Couplers** | Temperature/pressure control | `AndersenThermostat`, `BerendsenBarostat` |
| **Loggers** | Data collection | `TemperatureLogger`, `CoordinatesLogger` |

Sources: [src/types.jl](src/types.jl#L1-L80), [src/simulators.jl](src/simulators.jl#L1-L50), [src/coupling.jl](src/coupling.jl#L1-L70)

## Advanced Example: Protein Simulation on GPU

Scale up to realistic molecular systems using Molly's GPU acceleration. This simulates a protein with explicit water using particle mesh Ewald electrostatics.

```julia
using Molly, CUDA

# Access included force field data
data_dir = joinpath(dirname(pathof(Molly)), "..", "data")

# Load force field from OpenMM XML files
ff = MolecularForceField(
    Float32,  # Use single precision for GPU
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "ff99SBildn.xml"),
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "tip3p_standard.xml"),
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "his.xml"),
)

# Load protein structure from PDB file
sys = System(
    joinpath(data_dir, "6mrr_equil.pdb"),
    ff;
    nonbonded_method=:pme,        # Particle mesh Ewald
    loggers=(
        energy=TotalEnergyLogger(10),
        writer=TrajectoryWriter(10, "traj_6mrr.dcd"),
    ),
    array_type=CuArray,            # Use GPU arrays
)

# Energy minimization
minimizer = SteepestDescentMinimizer()
simulate!(sys, minimizer)

# Set temperature and initialize velocities
temp = Float32(298.0)u"K"
random_velocities!(sys, temp)

# Configure Langevin dynamics with pressure control
simulator = Langevin(
    dt=Float32(0.001)u"ps",
    temperature=temp,
    friction=Float32(1.0)u"ps^-1",
    coupling=MonteCarloBarostat(Float32(1.0)u"bar", temp, sys.boundary),
)

# Run production simulation
simulate!(sys, simulator, 5_000)
```

This 5 picosecond simulation demonstrates Molly's capability to handle complex biomolecular systems with realistic force fields. The output trajectory file can be visualized in PyMOL or other MD viewers.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L74-L107), [src/setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L1-L60), [src/interactions/ewald.jl](src/interactions/ewald.jl)

> [!TIP]
> **Performance Tip**: Use `Float32` instead of `Float64` on GPUs for 2-3x speedup with minimal accuracy loss. Set `array_type=CuArray` when using CUDA for automatic GPU acceleration.

## Simulation Workflow Overview

Molly simulations follow a consistent pattern that adapts to your specific scientific questions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Phase1["1. System Setup"]
        A1[Define Boundary<br/>periodic box type]
        A2[Create Atoms<br/>mass, interactions]
        A3[Place Atoms<br/>coordinates & topology]
    end
    
    subgraph Phase2["2. Force Configuration"]
        B1[Pairwise Interactions<br/>LJ, Coulomb, etc.]
        B2[Specific Interactions<br/>bonds, angles, torsions]
        B3[Neighbor Finder<br/>optimize calculations]
    end
    
    subgraph Phase3["3. Initial Conditions"]
        C1[Initialize Velocities<br/>temperature]
        C2[Energy Minimization<br/>remove clashes]
        C3[Setup Loggers<br/>track observables]
    end
    
    subgraph Phase4["4. Simulation Control"]
        D1[Choose Integrator<br/>Verlet, Langevin]
        D2[Add Couplers<br/>thermostat, barostat]
        D3[Run Simulation<br/>evolve system]
    end
    
    subgraph Phase5["5. Analysis"]
        E1[Access Logged Data<br/>energies, trajectories]
        E2[Compute Observables<br/>RDF, correlations]
        E3[Visualize Results<br/>animations, plots]
    end
    
    Phase1 --> Phase2 --> Phase3 --> Phase4 --> Phase5
    
    style Phase1 fill:#fff3e0
    style Phase2 fill:#fff3e0
    style Phase3 fill:#fff3e0
    style Phase4 fill:#e8f5e9
    style Phase5 fill:#e3f2fd
```

Sources: [test/basic.jl](test/basic.jl#L100-L180), [test/simulation.jl](test/simulation.jl#L1-L80)

## Available Features

Molly provides a comprehensive toolkit for molecular simulation:

### Interactions
| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **Non-bonded** | Lennard-Jones, Coulomb, electrostatics, PME, soft sphere, Mie, Buckingham |
| **Bonded** | Harmonic/Morse bonds, bond angles, torsion angles, position restraints, FENE bonds |
| **Implicit Solvent** | GBSA methods for continuum solvent |

### Integrators & Couplers
| Component | Options |
|-----------|---------|
| **Integrators** | Verlet, Velocity Verlet, Störmer-Verlet, Langevin, Overdamped Langevin, Nosé-Hoover |
| **Thermostats** | Andersen, Berendsen, Velocity Rescaling, Immediate Rescaling |
| **Barostats** | C-rescale, Monte Carlo, Berendsen |

### Analysis & Output
- **Loggers**: Temperature, coordinates, velocities, energy, pressure, forces, time correlations
- **Trajectory Writing**: DCD, XTC, PDB, XYZ formats via Chemfiles.jl
- **Analysis**: RDF, energy conservation, structure analysis

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L38), [src/interactions/](src/interactions/), [src/loggers.jl](src/loggers.jl#L1-L80)

> [!TIP]
> **Differentiable Simulations**: Molly uniquely supports automatic differentiation through Enzyme.jl, enabling gradient-based force field optimization and inverse problems—perfect for machine learning applications in molecular science.

# Installation and Setup



Molly.jl is a pure Julia molecular dynamics simulation package designed for both computational efficiency and extensibility. This page guides you through installing Molly, configuring optional extensions for GPU acceleration and visualization, and verifying your setup to ensure everything is ready for molecular dynamics simulations.

## Prerequisites

Before installing Molly, you need to have Julia installed on your system. **Julia 1.10 or later is required** to access the latest features and compatibility improvements of Molly [Project.toml#L87](Project.toml#L87-L87). The package is designed to work with the current stable Julia release for optimal performance. Molly has been tested and is actively developed on Julia versions 1.10 and above, taking advantage of language improvements in recent Julia releases.

Sources: [Project.toml](Project.toml#L87), [README.md](README.md#L63)

## Basic Installation

Installing Molly is straightforward through Julia's built-in package manager. Enter the Julia REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) and press `]` to enter package mode, then execute the installation command:

```julia
] add Molly
```

This command downloads and installs Molly along with its core dependencies. The installation process automatically resolves and installs all required packages from the Julia General registry. The core installation includes essential computational libraries such as:

- **StaticArrays.jl** for efficient array operations
- **Unitful.jl** and **UnitfulAtomic.jl** for physical unit handling
- **CellListMap.jl** for optimized neighbor searching
- **AtomsBase.jl** and **AtomsCalculators.jl** for interoperability
- **FFTW.jl** for Fast Fourier Transform operations
- **Graphs.jl** for topology management

![Molly Logo](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/blob/master/docs/src/images/logo_molly.png)

Sources: [Project.toml](Project.toml#L9-L38), [README.md](README.md#L63-L67)

## Optional Extensions and GPU Support

Molly provides optional extensions that enable advanced capabilities such as GPU acceleration, automatic differentiation, visualization, and additional analysis tools. These extensions are not installed by default to keep the base installation lightweight, but can be added based on your specific needs.

### GPU Acceleration

For running simulations on GPU hardware, Molly supports multiple GPU backends through the KernelAbstractions.jl interface. To enable GPU support, install the appropriate package for your hardware:

| Hardware | Required Package | Array Type | Performance Notes |
|----------|------------------|------------|-------------------|
| NVIDIA GPU | `CUDA` | `CuArray` | Best performance, warp-optimized kernels |
| AMD GPU | `AMDGPU` | `ROCArray` | Functional via KernelAbstractions |
| Intel GPU | `oneAPI` | `oneArray` | Functional via KernelAbstractions |
| Apple Silicon | `Metal` | `MtlArray` | Requires Float32 precision only |

To install CUDA support for NVIDIA GPUs:
```julia
] add Molly CUDA
```

The MollyCUDAExt extension provides specialized CUDA kernels that use warp-level features for optimal performance [ext/MollyCUDAExt.jl#L1-L15](ext/MollyCUDAExt.jl#L1-L15). For Apple Silicon devices, Metal support requires using `Float32` precision due to hardware limitations [docs/src/documentation.md#L126-L127](docs/src/documentation.md#L126-L127).

Sources: [Project.toml](Project.toml#L41-L48), [ext/MollyCUDAExt.jl](ext/MollyCUDAExt.jl#L1-L15), [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L126-L127)

### Visualization and Analysis

For creating animations and visualizing simulation trajectories, install GLMakie for GPU-accelerated rendering:

```julia
] add Molly GLMakie Colors
```

The MollyGLMakieExt extension enables the `visualize` function for saving trajectory animations in various video formats [Project.toml#L49-L49](Project.toml#L49-L49).

For additional analysis capabilities, you can install:

- **Enzyme.jl**: For automatic differentiation through simulations (`add Molly Enzyme`)
- **KernelDensity.jl**: For kernel density estimation functions (`add Molly KernelDensity`)
- **PythonCall.jl**: For interfacing with Python libraries like ASE (`add Molly PythonCall`)

Sources: [Project.toml](Project.toml#L49-L56), [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L170-L173)

## Architecture Overview

Molly follows a **modular architecture** that allows you to use components as defined by the package or define your own versions. The system is built around several core abstractions:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Core System"
        A[System Object] --> B[Atoms]
        A --> C[Coordinates]
        A --> D[Velocities]
        A --> E[Boundary]
        A --> F[Interactions]
        A --> G[Loggers]
    end
    
    subgraph "Simulation Layer"
        H[Simulator] --> I[Integrator]
        H --> J[Thermostat]
        H --> K[Barostat]
        H --> L[Neighbor Finder]
    end
    
    subgraph "Optional Extensions"
        M[CUDA Extension]
        N[Enzyme Extension]
        O[GLMakie Extension]
    end
    
    A --> H
    F --> L
    M -.-> H
    N -.-> F
    O -.-> G
    
    style A fill:#e1f5ff
    style H fill:#fff4e1
    style M fill:#ffe1f5
    style N fill:#ffe1f5
    style O fill:#ffe1f5
```

The central **System object** contains all simulation state, while the **Simulator** controls the time evolution. Interactions can be pairwise (non-bonded) or specific (bonds, angles, torsions). The extension system provides optional functionality without affecting core performance.

Sources: [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L8-L15), [Project.toml](Project.toml#L41-L56)

## Verification and Testing

After installation, verify that Molly is working correctly by running a simple simulation in the Julia REPL:

```julia
using Molly

# Create a simple Lennard-Jones fluid simulation
n_atoms = 100
boundary = CubicBoundary(2.0u"nm")
temp = 298.0u"K"
atom_mass = 10.0u"g/mol"

atoms = [Atom(mass=atom_mass, σ=0.3u"nm", ϵ=0.2u"kJ * mol^-1") for i in 1:n_atoms]
coords = place_atoms(n_atoms, boundary; min_dist=0.3u"nm")
velocities = [random_velocity(atom_mass, temp) for i in 1:n_atoms]

sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=(LennardJones(),),
    loggers=(temp=TemperatureLogger(10),),
)

simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.002u"ps",
    coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 1.0u"ps"),
)

simulate!(sys, simulator, 1_000)
println("Simulation completed successfully!")
println("Final temperature: ", temperature(sys))
```

If you have GPU support installed, verify it works with this additional test:

```julia
using Molly, CUDA
n_atoms = 100
atom_mass = 10.0f0u"g/mol"
boundary = CubicBoundary(2.0f0u"nm")
atoms = CuArray([Atom(mass=atom_mass, σ=0.3f0u"nm", ϵ=0.2f0u"kJ * mol^-1") for i in 1:n_atoms])
coords = CuArray(place_atoms(n_atoms, boundary; min_dist=0.3u"nm"))
velocities = CuArray([random_velocity(atom_mass, temp) for i in 1:n_atoms])

sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=(LennardJones(),),
)

simulate!(deepcopy(sys), VelocityVerlet(dt=0.002f0u"ps"), 20)  # Compilation
simulate!(sys, VelocityVerlet(dt=0.002f0u"ps"), 100)       # Run
println("GPU simulation completed!")
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L69-L95), [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L139-L165)

## Configuration Options

Molly provides several environment variables for fine-tuning performance, particularly for GPU operations:

| Environment Variable | Purpose | Default | When to Adjust |
|---------------------|---------|---------|----------------|
| `MOLLY_GPUNTHREADS_PAIRWISE` | GPU threads for pairwise interactions | Auto-configured | GPU memory errors |
| `MOLLY_GPUNTHREADS_SPECIFIC` | GPU threads for specific interactions | Auto-configured | GPU memory errors |
| `MOLLY_GPUNTHREADS_DISTANCENF` | GPU threads for distance-based neighbor finding | Auto-configured | GPU memory errors |
| `MOLLY_GPUNTHREADS_IMPLICIT` | GPU threads for implicit solvent calculations | Auto-configured | GPU memory errors |
| `JULIA_NUM_THREADS` | CPU threads for parallel execution | Available cores | Thread contention issues |

> [!TIP]
> Only adjust GPU thread environment variables if you encounter out-of-memory errors on smaller GPUs. The default configuration is optimized for most use cases.

CPU threading can be controlled by passing `n_threads` to the `simulate!` function. Setting `n_threads=1` disables parallelization, while values greater than the number of available threads may sometimes improve performance [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L112-L117).

Sources: [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L197-L202), [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L112-L117)

Molly.jl/

The `data/` directory contains force field files (ff99SBildn, TIP3P water) and example structures that are referenced in the documentation. These files are useful for testing your installation and learning the package workflows.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L40)

## Common Troubleshooting

### Installation Issues

If you encounter problems during installation, try the following steps:

1. **Update Julia and packages**: Ensure you're using Julia 1.10 or later and update your package registry:
   ```julia
   ] up
   ```

2. **Clean environment**: If dependency conflicts occur, create a fresh environment:
   ```julia
   ] activate --temp
   ] add Molly
   ```

3. **Precompilation issues**: Force recompilation of problematic packages:
   ```julia
   ] build Molly
   ```

### GPU Setup Issues

For GPU-related problems:

- Verify CUDA is properly installed on your system with `using CUDA; CUDA.versioninfo()`
- Check that your GPU driver is up to date
- Ensure you're using compatible CUDA versions (4.2 or 5.x as specified in Project.toml)
- For Apple Silicon, confirm you're using Float32 precision in all calculations

### Performance Issues

If simulations run slowly:

- Verify threading is enabled by checking `Threads.nthreads()`
- Start Julia with appropriate thread count: `julia --threads auto`
- For GPU simulations, ensure arrays are moved to GPU before simulation
- Consider using `Float32` for better GPU performance when numerical precision permits

> [!TIP]
> Always run a brief "warmup" simulation (e.g., 20-50 steps) before benchmarking. This allows Julia's JIT compiler to optimize the code and gives accurate performance measurements.

Sources: [Project.toml](Project.toml#L62-L66), [docs/src/documentation.md](docs/src/documentation.md#L194-L195)

# Lennard-Jones Fluid Simulation



A Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluid is one of the simplest and most important models in molecular dynamics. It describes the behavior of neutral atoms interacting through van der Waals forces, capturing both **short-range repulsion** (preventing atoms from overlapping) and **long-range attraction** (causing atoms to cluster). This tutorial will guide you through simulating a Lennard-Jones fluid using Molly.jl, from setup to analysis.

## Understanding the Lennard-Jones Potential

The Lennard-Jones 6-12 potential models the interaction energy between two neutral atoms as a function of their separation distance. The mathematical form is:

```math
V(r_{ij}) = 4\varepsilon_{ij} \left[\left(\frac{\sigma_{ij}}{r_{ij}}\right)^{12} - \left(\frac{\sigma_{ij}}{r_{ij}}\right)^{6}\right]
```

Where:
- **σ (sigma)**: The distance at which the inter-particle potential is zero, representing the finite size of atoms
- **ε (epsilon)**: The depth of the potential well, representing the strength of attraction
- **r**: The separation distance between atom pairs

The **r⁻¹² term** dominates at short distances, providing strong repulsion as atoms approach each other. The **r⁻⁶ term** dominates at longer distances, providing weak attraction. This creates a potential energy curve with a minimum that determines the equilibrium separation distance.

## Architecture Overview

Before diving into the code, let's understand how Molly.jl organizes a Lennard-Jones fluid simulation:

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Simulation Components] --> B[System State]
    A --> C[Interactions]
    A --> D[Integrator]
    A --> E[Thermostat]
    A --> F[Loggers]
    
    B --> B1[Atoms<br/>mass, σ, ε]
    B --> B2[Coordinates]
    B --> B3[Velocities]
    B --> B4[Boundary<br/>Periodic]
    
    C --> C1[LennardJones<br/>PairwiseInteraction]
    C --> C2[Cutoff Strategy<br/>DistanceCutoff]
    C --> C3[Mixing Rules<br/>Lorentz/Geometric]
    
    D --> D1[VelocityVerlet<br/>dt=0.002ps]
    
    E --> E1[AndersenThermostat<br/>T=298K]
    
    F --> F1[TemperatureLogger<br/>n_steps=100]
    
    C1 --> G[simulate!<br/>Main Loop]
    D1 --> G
    E1 --> G
    F1 --> G
    
    G --> H[Output<br/>Trajectory Data]
```

This modular design allows you to mix and match components while keeping the simulation logic clean and maintainable.

## Complete Lennard-Jones Fluid Simulation

Here's a complete, runnable example that simulates a Lennard-Jones fluid with 100 atoms:

```julia
using Molly
using Unitful

# Simulation parameters
n_atoms = 100
boundary = CubicBoundary(2.0u"nm")
temp = 298.0u"K"
atom_mass = 10.0u"g/mol"

# Create atoms with Lennard-Jones parameters
atoms = [Atom(mass=atom_mass, σ=0.3u"nm", ϵ=0.2u"kJ * mol^-1") for i in 1:n_atoms]

# Place atoms randomly with minimum distance constraint
coords = place_atoms(n_atoms, boundary; min_dist=0.3u"nm")

# Initialize velocities from Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
velocities = [random_velocity(atom_mass, temp) for i in 1:n_atoms]

# Define pairwise interactions
pairwise_inters = (LennardJones(),)

# Create simulator with time step and thermostat
simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.002u"ps",
    coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 1.0u"ps"),
)

# Set up system with all components
sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=pairwise_inters,
    loggers=(temp=TemperatureLogger(100),),
)

# Run simulation for 10,000 steps
simulate!(sys, simulator, 10_000)

# Access temperature data
temp_history = values(sys.loggers.temp)
println("Final temperature: ", last(temp_history))
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L43-L74), [lennard_jones.jl](src/interactions/lennard_jones.jl#L1-L51), [setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L18-L61), [simulators.jl](src/simulators.jl#L1-L100), [types.jl](src/types.jl#L200-L256), [loggers.jl](src/loggers.jl#L1-L100)

## Step-by-Step Simulation Workflow

The following flowchart illustrates the complete process from setup to analysis:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[Start Simulation] --> A[Define Parameters<br/>n_atoms, T, mass]
    A --> B[Create Atoms<br/>Set σ and ε]
    B --> C[Place Atoms<br/>place_atoms with min_dist]
    C --> D[Initialize Velocities<br/>Maxwell-Boltzmann]
    D --> E[Set Up Interactions<br/>LennardJones]
    E --> F[Choose Simulator<br/>VelocityVerlet with dt]
    F --> G[Add Thermostat<br/>AndersenThermostat]
    G --> H[Configure Loggers<br/>TemperatureLogger]
    H --> I[Build System<br/>System constructor]
    I --> J[Run Simulation<br/>simulate!]
    J --> K[Analyze Results<br/>Process logger data]
    K --> End[End]
```

Let's examine each step in detail.

## Defining Simulation Parameters

The first step is to define the fundamental parameters that characterize your system:

```julia
n_atoms = 100                    # Number of particles
boundary = CubicBoundary(2.0u"nm")  # Periodic boundary box size
temp = 298.0u"K"                 # Target temperature
atom_mass = 10.0u"g/mol"         # Mass of each atom
```

The **CubicBoundary** creates a periodic box with 2.0 nm side length. Periodic boundary conditions are essential for simulating bulk fluids, as they eliminate surface effects and allow atoms to wrap around when they exit one side of the box. Molly.jl automatically handles coordinate wrapping during the simulation.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L46-L49), [types.jl](src/types.jl#L200-L256), [setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L18-L61)

## Creating Atoms with Lennard-Jones Parameters

Each atom in the simulation requires mass and Lennard-Jones parameters:

```julia
atoms = [Atom(mass=atom_mass, σ=0.3u"nm", ϵ=0.2u"kJ * mol^-1") for i in 1:n_atoms]
```

The **Atom** struct stores the physical properties needed for simulation:
- **mass**: Atomic mass in g/mol
- **σ (sigma)**: Distance at which potential is zero (0.3 nm)
- **ε (epsilon)**: Depth of potential well (0.2 kJ/mol)

These parameters determine how atoms interact. Larger σ values create "bigger" atoms, while larger ε values create stronger attractions. When atoms of different types interact, Molly.jl automatically computes combined parameters using mixing rules.

Sources: [types.jl](src/types.jl#L200-L256), [lennard_jones.jl](src/interactions/lennard_jones.jl#L28-L51)

## Parameter Reference Table

| Parameter | Symbol | Typical Range | Physical Meaning |
|-----------|--------|----------------|------------------|
| Mass | m | 1-200 g/mol | Inertia of particles |
| Sigma | σ | 0.2-0.4 nm | Van der Waals radius |
| Epsilon | ε | 0.1-1.0 kJ/mol | Interaction strength |
| Temperature | T | 100-500 K | Thermal energy |
| Time step | dt | 0.001-0.005 ps | Integration precision |
| Cutoff distance | rc | 1.0-1.5 nm | Interaction range |

## Placing Atoms in the Simulation Box

The `place_atoms` function randomly distributes atoms while maintaining minimum separation:

```julia
coords = place_atoms(n_atoms, boundary; min_dist=0.3u"nm")
```

This function:
1. Attempts to place atoms at random coordinates within the boundary
2. Ensures no two atoms are closer than `min_dist` (accounting for periodic boundaries)
3. Tries up to `max_attempts` times before failing

The **min_dist** parameter should be set to approximately the σ value to prevent atoms from starting in highly repulsive configurations, which would cause numerical instability. For better performance, you can increase this value to match the equilibrium distance (~2^(1/6) × σ ≈ 1.12 × σ).

Sources: [setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L18-L61)

## Initializing Velocities

Velocities are initialized from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at the target temperature:

```julia
velocities = [random_velocity(atom_mass, temp) for i in 1:n_atoms]
```

This function generates random velocities that follow the equilibrium distribution for the specified mass and temperature. The distribution accounts for the different thermal energy in each degree of freedom, ensuring realistic starting conditions. Over time, the velocities will redistribute according to the interactions and thermostat.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L50-L51)

## Configuring Lennard-Jones Interactions

The `LennardJones` struct defines the pairwise interaction model:

```julia
pairwise_inters = (LennardJones(),)
```

By default, this creates a Lennard-Jones interaction with:
- **NoCutoff()**: Computes interactions for all atom pairs (suitable for small systems)
- **lorentz_σ_mixing**: Arithmetic mean of σ values (σ_ij = (σ_i + σ_j) / 2)
- **geometric_ϵ_mixing**: Geometric mean of ε values (ε_ij = √(ε_i × ε_j))
- **lj_zero_shortcut**: Skips computation if ε or σ is zero

For larger systems, you can add a cutoff distance:

```julia
pairwise_inters = (LennardJones(cutoff=DistanceCutoff(1.0u"nm")),)
```

This sets forces and potential energy to zero for atom pairs separated by more than 1.0 nm, dramatically improving computational efficiency. You can also use **ShiftedPotentialCutoff** or **ShiftedForceCutoff** for smoother cutoffs that improve energy conservation.

Sources: [lennard_jones.jl](src/interactions/lennard_jones.jl#L1-L88), [cutoffs.jl](src/cutoffs.jl#L1-L100)

## Choosing the Integration Method

The **Velocity Verlet** integrator is the standard choice for molecular dynamics:

```julia
simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.002u"ps",
    coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 1.0u"ps"),
)
```

**Velocity Verlet** provides:
- **Second-order accuracy** in time integration
- **Symplectic** properties that conserve energy in the absence of a thermostat
- **Time-reversibility** for better numerical stability

The **dt parameter** (0.002 ps = 2 femtoseconds) must be small enough to resolve the fastest vibrations in the system. A good rule of thumb is to ensure dt is at least 10-20 times smaller than the characteristic vibration timescale.

Sources: [simulators.jl](src/simulators.jl#L1-L100)

## Controlling Temperature with a Thermostat

The **Andersen thermostat** maintains the system at constant temperature:

```julia
coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 1.0u"ps")
```

This thermostat works by:
1. Occasionally selecting random atoms
2. Reassigning their velocities from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at T
3. Applying this with a characteristic time scale (1.0 ps)

The coupling parameter controls how often atoms are affected—smaller values mean more frequent velocity reassignments. This creates a canonical (NVT) ensemble where temperature fluctuates around the target value.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L52-L55), [coupling.jl](src/coupling.jl) (not viewed but referenced in examples)

## Setting Up Data Loggers

Loggers collect simulation data at regular intervals:

```julia
loggers=(temp=TemperatureLogger(100),)
```

The **TemperatureLogger** records system temperature every 100 steps. Available loggers include:

| Logger | Records | Typical Usage |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| TemperatureLogger | Kinetic temperature | Thermostat validation |
| CoordinatesLogger | Atom positions | Trajectory analysis |
| TotalEnergyLogger | Total energy | Conservation checks |
| KineticEnergyLogger | Kinetic energy | Energy distribution |
| PotentialEnergyLogger | Potential energy | Interaction analysis |
| ForcesLogger | Forces on atoms | Structural properties |

Loggers store data efficiently and can be accessed after simulation using `values(logger)`.

Sources: [loggers.jl](src/loggers.jl#L1-L100), [examples.md](docs/src/examples.md#L23-L32)

## Assembling the System

All components are combined into a `System` object:

```julia
sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=pairwise_inters,
    loggers=(temp=TemperatureLogger(100),),
)
```

The `System` struct is the central data structure that holds all simulation state. It contains:
- **atoms**: Array of Atom objects with masses and interaction parameters
- **coords**: Current positions of all atoms
- **boundary**: Periodic boundary conditions
- **velocities**: Current velocities of all atoms
- **pairwise_inters**: Tuple of pairwise interactions (can include LennardJones, Coulomb, etc.)
- **loggers**: Named tuple of loggers for data collection

This design makes it easy to pass the entire system state to simulation functions and analysis routines.

Sources: [types.jl](src/types.jl#L100-L200), [README.md](README.md#L57-L66)

## Running the Simulation

The `simulate!` function executes the simulation:

```julia
simulate!(sys, simulator, 10_000)
```

This runs the simulation for 10,000 time steps (20 ps total). During execution:

1. **Forces** are computed from Lennard-Jones interactions
2. **Velocities** are updated using the integration scheme
3. **Positions** are updated based on velocities
4. **Thermostat** applies temperature control
5. **Boundary conditions** wrap coordinates as needed
6. **Loggers** record data at specified intervals

The exclamation mark (!) indicates that this function modifies the system state in place, which is the standard Julia convention for in-place operations.

Sources: [simulators.jl](src/simulators.jl#L28-L100), [README.md](README.md#L68-L69)

## Accessing and Analyzing Results

After simulation completion, retrieve logged data:

```julia
temp_history = values(sys.loggers.temp)
println("Final temperature: ", last(temp_history))
println("Average temperature: ", mean(temp_history))
println("Temperature std dev: ", std(temp_history))

# You can also access the final system state
final_coords = sys.coords
final_velocities = sys.velocities
```

The logger returns a vector of temperature values sampled at regular intervals. You can compute statistics, create plots, or perform further analysis. For example, temperature fluctuations can indicate whether the thermostat is working correctly.

For more sophisticated analysis, consider adding additional loggers such as **PotentialEnergyLogger** to track energy changes, or **CoordinatesLogger** to record trajectories for visualization.

Sources: [loggers.jl](src/loggers.jl#L1-L100)

## Advanced Configuration: Using Neighbor Lists

For systems with more than ~100 atoms, computing all pairwise interactions becomes expensive. You can optimize performance using neighbor lists:

```julia
# Configure Lennard-Jones with neighbor list support
lj = LennardJones(
    cutoff=DistanceCutoff(1.0u"nm"),
    use_neighbors=true,
)

# Set up neighbor finder
neighbor_finder = DistanceNeighborFinder(
    eligible=trues(n_atoms, n_atoms),
    n_steps=10,
    dist_cutoff=1.1u"nm",
)

# Create system with neighbor finder
sys = System(
    atoms=atoms,
    coords=coords,
    boundary=boundary,
    velocities=velocities,
    pairwise_inters=(lj,),
    neighbor_finder=neighbor_finder,
    loggers=(temp=TemperatureLogger(100),),
)
```

The **neighbor finder** builds a list of atom pairs within the cutoff distance and updates this list periodically (every 10 steps in this example). This reduces the computational complexity from O(n²) to O(n) for large systems.

The **dist_cutoff** for the neighbor finder should be slightly larger than the interaction cutoff to account for atom movement between updates.

Sources: [examples.md](docs/src/examples.md#L320-L344), [neighbors.jl](src/neighbors.jl) (not viewed but referenced)

## Common Issues and Troubleshooting

| Issue | Symptoms | Solution |
|-------|----------|----------|
| Atoms explode | High energy, NaN values | Decrease dt or increase min_dist |
| Temperature drift | System heating/cooling | Check thermostat coupling strength |
| Poor energy conservation | Energy drift over time | Use ShiftedForceCutoff or smaller dt |
| Slow performance | Long computation time | Add neighbor lists for large systems |
| Periodic artifacts | Non-physical behavior | Increase box size or use triclinic boundary |

> [!TIP]
> Always verify your simulation by checking that temperature stabilizes and energy is conserved (without thermostat) over short test runs before committing to long production simulations.

## Visualization and Further Analysis

While this example focuses on a simple temperature logger, you can extend your analysis by:

1. **Adding coordinate logging**: Use `CoordinatesLogger(10)` to record atom positions every 10 steps
2. **Computing radial distribution functions**: Analyze structure using RDF calculations
3. **Visualizing trajectories**: Use Makie.jl or external tools like VMD or PyMOL
4. **Calculating transport properties**: Measure diffusion coefficients from mean-squared displacement

For more complex simulations including bonded interactions, electrostatic forces, or implicit solvent, explore the [Protein Simulation Setup](5-protein-simulation-setup) example.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L40), [analysis.jl](src/analysis.jl) (not viewed but available)

# Protein Simulation Setup



This guide teaches you how to set up and run molecular dynamics simulations of proteins using Molly.jl. You'll learn to load protein structures from standard files, apply molecular force fields, configure simulation parameters, and track system properties through logging.

![Protein Simulation](https://github.com/JuliaMolSim/Molly.jl/blob/master/docs/src/images/sim_6mrr.gif)

Protein simulations in Molly leverage industry-standard file formats and force fields, making it straightforward to transition from other MD packages. The system automatically reads atomic coordinates from structure files and force field parameters from OpenMM-compatible XML files, constructing a complete simulation-ready system with minimal configuration.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L80), [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L1-L100)

## Understanding Protein Simulation Architecture

Setting up a protein simulation involves coordinating multiple components that work together to create a physically accurate molecular system. The architecture follows a dataflow pattern where structural data and force field parameters converge into a unified System object, which is then evolved through time using integrators and coupled to environmental controls.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Coordinate File<br/>PDB or GRO] -->|Read atomic positions| B[System Constructor]
    C[Force Field Files<br/>XML format] -->|Parse parameters| B
    D[Simulation Options<br/>nonbonded_method, boundary] --> B
    B --> E[Complete System]
    E -->|Initialize| F[Integrator<br/>VelocityVerlet, Langevin]
    E -->|Attach| G[Coupling<br/>Thermostat, Barostat]
    E -->|Configure| H[Loggers<br/>Temperature, Energy, Coords]
    F -->|Evolve| I[Simulation Loop]
    G -->|Control| I
    H -->|Monitor| I
    I --> J[Output<br/>Trajectories, Analysis]
```

This architecture separates concerns cleanly: coordinate files provide atomic positions, force field files define interaction parameters, and simulation options control the computational approach. The System constructor orchestrates these inputs, automatically generating atomic properties, interaction lists, and topology information.

Sources: [src/types.jl](src/types.jl#L500-L650), [src/setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L600-L900)

## Loading Protein Structures

Molly supports loading protein structures from multiple file formats through the Chemfiles.jl interface. The two most commonly used formats are PDB (Protein Data Bank) and GRO (GROMACS coordinate format). When constructing a System from files, you simply provide the file paths, and Molly automatically parses the structure.

**Basic protein system setup:**

```julia
using Molly

# Define paths to your data
data_dir = joinpath(dirname(pathof(Molly)), "..", "data")

# Load a protein structure and force field
ff = MolecularForceField(
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "ff99SBildn.xml"),
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "tip3p_standard.xml"),
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "his.xml"),
)

sys = System(
    joinpath(data_dir, "6mrr_equil.pdb"),
    ff;
    nonbonded_method=:cutoff,
    center_coords=false,
)
```

The System constructor automatically performs several key tasks:
- Parses atomic coordinates from the PDB file
- Matches each atom to its force field type based on residue and atom names
- Assigns masses, charges, and van der Waals parameters
- Constructs bonded interactions (bonds, angles, torsions)
- Sets up non-bonded interaction tables
- Determines molecular topology for neighbor finding

Sources: [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L57-L65), [src/setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L600-L799)

> [!TIP]
> The `center_coords=false` option preserves the original coordinates from your file. Setting `center_coords=true` (the default) shifts all coordinates so the system center is at the origin, which can improve numerical stability but may require re-positioning your protein in its solvent box.

## Working with Force Field Files

MolecularForceField objects parse OpenMM-style XML force field files to extract atom type definitions, residue templates, and interaction parameters. The most common force field combination for proteins in explicit solvent uses ff99SBildn for the protein and tip3p for water.

**Force field components:**

| Component | File Pattern | Purpose |
|-----------|--------------|---------|
| Protein force field | `ff99SBildn.xml` | Atom types, bonded parameters for amino acids |
| Water model | `tip3p_standard.xml` | TIP3P water parameters |
| Special residues | `his.xml` | Histidine protonation states and other special cases |

The MolecularForceField constructor automatically merges multiple XML files, handling conflicts according to standard rules. It reads:
- **AtomTypes**: Masses, element types, and initial parameter placeholders
- **Residues**: Atom type mappings and partial charges for each residue
- **HarmonicBondForce**: Bond equilibrium lengths and force constants
- **HarmonicAngleForce**: Angle equilibrium values and force constants
- **PeriodicTorsionForce**: Proper and improper torsion parameters with multiple periodicity terms
- **NonbondedForce**: Lennard-Jones σ and ε values, plus 1-4 scaling factors

Sources: [src/setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L130-L300), [data/force_fields](data/force_fields/)

## Configuring Non-Bonded Interactions

Non-bonded interactions—electrostatic and van der Waals forces—require special handling in protein simulations due to their computational cost. Molly provides multiple methods for calculating these interactions with different trade-offs between accuracy and performance.

**Non-bonded method comparison:**

| Method | Description | Use Case | Performance |
|--------|-------------|----------|-------------|
| `:cutoff` | Simple distance truncation | Small systems, testing | Fastest |
| `:pme` | Particle Mesh Ewald (approximate) | Production simulations, large systems | Fast, good accuracy |
| `:coul_pme` | PME with exact Coulomb | High-precision requirements | Slower, most accurate |

```julia
# Cutoff method for quick tests
sys_cutoff = System(coords_file, ff; nonbonded_method=:cutoff)

# PME method for production runs
sys_pme = System(coords_file, ff; nonbonded_method=:pme)

# PME with exact Coulomb for validation
sys_exact = System(coords_file, ff; nonbonded_method=:pme, approximate_pme=false)
```

The PME method splits electrostatic calculations into direct real-space interactions (treated with a cutoff) and reciprocal-space calculations handled via Fast Fourier Transforms. This approach provides O(N log N) scaling instead of O(N²), making it feasible for large biomolecular systems.

Sources: [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L66-L72), [README.md](README.md#L1-L80)

## Setting Up Simulation Controls

Protein simulations require careful control of temperature and pressure to maintain physically realistic conditions. Molly provides multiple thermostats and barostats that can be combined with integrators to create complete simulation environments.

**Complete simulation setup with coupling:**

```julia
# System parameters
temp = 298.0u"K"
press = 1.0u"bar"

# Create integrator with thermostat coupling
simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.0005u"ps",
    coupling=AndersenThermostat(temp, 10.0u"ps")
)

# Or combine thermostat and barostat
thermostat = AndersenThermostat(temp, 10.0u"ps")
barostat = MonteCarloBarostat(press, temp, sys.boundary; n_steps=20)
simulator = VelocityVerlet(
    dt=0.0002u"ps",
    coupling=(thermostat, barostat)
)

# Initialize velocities at target temperature
random_velocities!(sys, temp)

# Run simulation
simulate!(sys, simulator, n_steps; n_threads=Threads.nthreads())
```

**Available thermostats:**
- **AndersenThermostat**: Random velocity rescaling with specified collision frequency
- **BerendsenThermostat**: Exponential relaxation toward target temperature
- **VelocityRescaling**: Modified Berendsen with correct fluctuation properties

**Available barostats:**
- **MonteCarloBarostat**: Stochastic volume changes
- **BerendsenBarostat**: Exponential pressure relaxation
- **CRescaleBarostat**: Correct volume fluctuation statistics

Sources: [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L12-L13), [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L60-L75)

## Logging and Trajectory Output

Tracking simulation properties is essential for analysis and debugging. Molly provides a flexible logger system that can record various system properties at specified intervals, including writing trajectory files for visualization.

**Comprehensive logging setup:**

```julia
using Molly

# Configure loggers to record every 10 steps
sys = System(
    coords_file,
    ff;
    loggers=(
        temp=TemperatureLogger(10),           # Temperature history
        coords=CoordinatesLogger(10),         # All atomic coordinates
        energy=TotalEnergyLogger(10),         # Total system energy
        density=DensityLogger(10),            # System density
    ),
    nonbonded_method=:cutoff,
)

# Add trajectory writers
dcd_file = "trajectory.dcd"
pdb_file = "trajectory.pdb"

sys = System(
    coords_file,
    ff;
    loggers=(
        # ... existing loggers ...
        dcd_writer=TrajectoryWriter(10, dcd_file; atom_inds=1001:2000),
        pdb_writer=TrajectoryWriter(10, pdb_file),
    ),
    nonbonded_method=:cutoff,
)

# After simulation, access logged data
temperatures = values(sys.loggers.temp)
energies = values(sys.loggers.energy)
```

The TrajectoryWriter supports multiple formats through Chemfiles.jl, including DCD (for large trajectories), PDB (for visualization and analysis), and XTC (compressed trajectories). The `atom_inds` parameter allows you to write only a subset of atoms, useful for focusing on specific regions like a protein's binding site.

Sources: [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L4-L11), [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L28-L39)

## Complete Protein Simulation Example

Putting all components together, here's a complete workflow for simulating a protein with solvent:

```julia
using Molly

# 1. Set up data paths
data_dir = joinpath(dirname(pathof(Molly)), "..", "data")

# 2. Load force field
ff = MolecularForceField(
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "ff99SBildn.xml"),
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "tip3p_standard.xml"),
    joinpath(data_dir, "force_fields", "his.xml"),
)

# 3. Create system with logging
sys = System(
    joinpath(data_dir, "6mrr_equil.pdb"),
    ff;
    nonbonded_method=:pme,
    loggers=(
        temp=TemperatureLogger(100),
        energy=TotalEnergyLogger(100),
        coords=CoordinatesLogger(100),
    ),
    center_coords=false,
)

# 4. Energy minimization (important starting step)
minimizer = SteepestDescentMinimizer()
simulate!(sys, minimizer)

# 5. Initialize velocities
random_velocities!(sys, 298.0u"K")

# 6. Set up simulator with thermostat
simulator = Langevin(
    dt=0.0005u"ps",
    temperature=298.0u"K",
    friction=1.0u"ps^-1",
)

# 7. Run production simulation
simulate!(sys, simulator, 10_000; n_threads=Threads.nthreads())

# 8. Analyze results
println("Final temperature: ", temperature(sys))
println("Energy conservation: ", last(values(sys.loggers.energy)))
```

This complete workflow demonstrates best practices: energy minimization before dynamics to remove bad contacts, proper thermostat setup for temperature control, and logging for post-simulation analysis.

Sources: [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L57-L100), [docs/src/examples.md](docs/src/examples.md#L1-L50)

## Performance Optimization Options

Protein simulations can be computationally intensive. Molly provides several optimization options that can dramatically improve performance without significantly affecting accuracy.

**Performance configuration matrix:**

| Configuration | Float Type | Units | GPU | Speed vs. Reference |
|---------------|------------|-------|-----|---------------------|
| Baseline | Float64 | Yes | CPU | 1.0x |
| Float32 | Float32 | Yes | CPU | ~2x faster |
| No units | Float64 | No | CPU | ~1.5x faster |
| Float32 + no units | Float32 | No | CPU | ~3x faster |
| GPU (CUDA) | Float64 | Yes | CUDA | ~5x faster |
| GPU Float32 | Float32 | Yes | CUDA | ~10x faster |

```julia
# Optimized setup for production runs
sys = System(
    Float32,  # Use Float32 for better GPU performance
    coords_file,
    ff;
    units=false,  # Disable units for speed
    array_type=CuArray,  # Use GPU arrays
    dist_cutoff=1.0,  # No units needed when units=false
    nonbonded_method=:cutoff,
)

# Run with optimal settings
simulate!(sys, simulator, n_steps; n_threads=Threads.nthreads())
```

> [!TIP]
> For large-scale production simulations, Float32 on GPU typically offers the best performance-to-accuracy ratio. Test your system with both Float64 and Float32 to ensure the reduced precision doesn't affect your specific observables of interest.

Sources: [benchmark/protein.jl](benchmark/protein.jl#L1-L62), [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L45-L60)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

When setting up protein simulations, you may encounter several common issues. Here are solutions to frequently encountered problems:

**Issue: "atom of type X has not had charge set"**
- **Cause**: Atom type in structure doesn't match force field definitions
- **Solution**: Verify residue names are standard (e.g., "ALA" not "ALA_N"), check force field includes all residues in your structure

**Issue: Poor energy conservation**
- **Cause**: Time step too large or system not minimized
- **Solution**: Reduce dt to 0.0005u"ps" or smaller, always run energy minimization before dynamics

**Issue: Simulation runs slowly**
- **Cause**: Using cutoff with large systems or inefficient parameters
- **Solution**: Switch to PME for electrostatics, enable GPU with Float32, use appropriate neighbor finder settings

**Issue: Pressure drifts in NPT simulation**
- **Cause**: Barostat relaxation time too short
- **Solution**: Increase `n_steps` parameter in MonteCarloBarostat to allow better equilibration

Sources: [src/setup.jl](src/setup.jl#L600-L650), [test/protein.jl](test/protein.jl#L100-L150)
